headline: Stellwagen Edge in 120 feet: cod stacked on the gravel, haddock chewing the mud
subhead: A soft neap tide has settled the bank down, and that's put steady groundfish in the box while the bluefin play hard to find.
body_markdown:
120 feet on the Stellwagen Edge, gravel bottom, and the rod tip is doing that short, stuttering bounce that means cod. That's where I've had my best mornings this week — the northern edge where the gravel patches run up against the sand, water column reading clean down to about 60 feet before it goes gray and cold. Bottom temp's still holding in the low 50s even with the surface pushing toward 68. That split is exactly what you want in the third week of July — warm water up top holding the bait, cold water down deep holding the fish that matter.

The cod have been on the smaller side but consistent — 3 to 8 pounds, a few better fish mixed in, taking clam bellies on a bucktail teaser rig fished tight to bottom. I'm not jigging hard out there right now, just lifting and dropping, letting the sinker find the gravel and feeling for that tick. The bigger fish have been coming off the steeper drops on the northeast corner of the Edge, where the gravel gives way fast into deeper water. If you're marking bait balls tight to bottom on the sounder, that's your spot — drop right through them.

Haddock have been the more reliable box-filler, and Middle Bank in 100 to 110 feet of mud has been the address. Diamond jigs with a green tube and a squid strip trailer have been doing the damage, worked with short, sharp lifts a foot or two off bottom. The neap tide we're sliding into off this first-quarter moon has actually helped here — less current means better bottom contact, less scope on the line, and the haddock have been stacking up thick enough that a good drift can put a dozen keepers in the cooler before you drift off the school. Tillies Bank has been giving up a similar mixed bag — haddock with some pollock mixed through the water column, especially up higher, 40 to 60 feet down, where the pollock like to hang off the structure edges chasing bait.

The bluefin have been the trickier story. We're seeing them — mackerel schools have been thick over the Basin and along the southern flank of the bank, and the whale activity out there has been about as good as I've seen it all year, humpbacks working sand eel pods right up on the surface in 90 to 120 feet of water off Tillies. Tuna are following that same bait, but they've been scattered and moving, not parked. Some days you run out and find them busting mackerel right on top and it's an easy troll pass with green machines and a spreader bar; other days you burn three hours covering the Basin and Carter Canyon approaches and never see a fin. That's the pattern coastwide right now with the trophy fishery closed since the start of the month — the slot fish, 27 inches up to just under 47, are around in decent numbers, but they're not holding still for anybody. Best luck has come to boats willing to run and gun off visible bird work and busting bait rather than anchoring on yesterday's numbers.

What's driving all of it is that soft current. First-quarter neap tides don't push bait the way a new or full moon does, so instead of getting concentrated pushes of sand eels and mackerel funneling through specific rips, we're getting looser, more spread-out bait fields — good for groundfish sitting tight to structure, tougher for tuna that want that bait pinned up against a hard edge. I'd expect that to change some as we build back toward the full moon at the end of the month, when the current picks back up and starts squeezing that bait tighter against the edges and canyons.

For this coming week, if I've only got one day, I'm starting on the Stellwagen Edge gravel early, working the cod bite before the sun gets high, then sliding over to Middle Bank for haddock on the back half of the tide once the current's really laid down. If the mackerel show thick and tight on the sounder anywhere along the southern flank, I'll pull the groundfish gear and put the troll spread out for an hour — those windows have been short but real. Carter Canyon's edge is worth a look too if you're running a bigger boat and want a shot at larger tuna passing through on the deeper contours, but I wouldn't build a whole day around it right now. Best case, the bait tightens up as we move off this neap and the bluefin start pinning against the edges again. If it stays loose and scattered like it has been, I'd rather bank a solid trip of cod and haddock than chase ghosts on the surface.
